EdgeCase is a graph analysis library for Python that pairs a fast Rust core with a friendly,
chainable API. Build a network, run any of more than 700 methods on it, query it with Cypher, and
get the answers back as Polars DataFrames and publication-ready pictures.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="assets/homepage/homepage.css">
<script src="assets/homepage/homepage.js" defer></script>
<script src="assets/homepage/backdrop.js" defer></script>
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import html
import json
from pathlib import Path

import great_docs as gd
from IPython.display import HTML

import edgecase as ec

gd.enable_tbl_preview(n_head=8, n_tail=3)


# What a query matched in `payments` (its nodes, and its edges in the order a walk along them
# would take), for the tour to light up in the graph
def _hits(query, nodes, edges):
    found = {}
    for kind, names in (("nodes", nodes), ("edges", edges)):
        payments.select_match(query, select=names)
        if kind == "nodes":
            found[kind] = [int(i) for i in payments.get_selected_node_ids()]
        else:
            found[kind] = [int(i) for i in payments.get_selected_edge_ids()]
        payments.clear_selection()
    ends = {
        row["id"]: (row["source"], row["target"])
        for row in payments.get_edge_df().select("id", "source", "target").iter_rows(named=True)
    }
    left = list(found["edges"])
    walk = []
    while left:
        after = [e for e in left if walk and ends[e][0] == ends[walk[-1]][1]]
        starts = [e for e in left if not any(ends[o][1] == ends[e][0] for o in left if o != e)]
        nxt = (after or starts or left)[0]
        walk.append(nxt)
        left.remove(nxt)
    found["edges"] = walk
    return HTML(f'<script type="application/json" class="ec-hits">{json.dumps(found)}</script>')
```

## An analysis, one step at a time {.ec-heading}

An analysis is a chain of methods on a graph, each storing its answer as a node or edge attribute
for the next to use. Step through this one, on the karate club network that Wayne Zachary studied
in the 1970s, to see what each step adds; the new lines of code are highlighted.

::::: {.ec-stepper}

:::: {.ec-step}
[Load]{.ec-step-name}

Start with a graph: here, one of the bundled datasets, the 34 members of a karate club and who
spent time with whom outside it.

```{python}
karate = (
    ec.karate_club()
)

karate.plot(
    label_by="label",
    seed=9,
)
```
::::

:::: {.ec-step}
[Communities]{.ec-step-name}

Find the club's communities with the Louvain method, and color the members by the one they're in.

```{python}
karate = (
    ec.karate_club()
    .cmty_louvain()
)

karate.plot(
    color_by="cmty_louvain",
    label_by="label",
    legend=False,
    seed=9,
)
```
::::

:::: {.ec-step}
[Centrality]{.ec-step-name}

Rank the members by PageRank and size them by it: the club's instructor (0) and its
administrator (33), at the centers of the two factions the club later split into, stand out.

```{python}
karate = (
    ec.karate_club()
    .cmty_louvain()
    .pagerank()
)

karate.plot(
    color_by="cmty_louvain",
    size_by="pagerank",
    label_by="label",
    legend=False,
    seed=9,
)
```
::::

:::: {.ec-step}
[Tabulate]{.ec-step-name}

Every answer is a column in the graph's node table, a Polars DataFrame, ready to sort, filter,
join, and export.

```{python}
karate = (
    ec.karate_club()
    .cmty_louvain()
    .pagerank()
)

(
    karate.get_node_df()
    .select("label", "role", "faction", "cmty_louvain", "pagerank")
    .sort("pagerank", descending=True)
)
```
::::

## Ask the graph with Cypher {.ec-heading}

Many questions about a network are questions about a shape: a ring of payments, everyone two
steps away, the shortest way through. [`match()`](reference/Graph.match.qmd) answers them with
Cypher, the pattern language of Neo4j, and returns what it finds as a DataFrame. Pick a query to
see its result, and what it matched in this small network of payments.

:::::: {.ec-tour}

::: {.ec-stage}
```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "How `payments` is made"
edges = [
    ("Dee", "Eve", 80), ("Eve", "Dee", 25), ("Ana", "Dee", 120), ("Dee", "Ben", 60),
    ("Ben", "Eve", 300), ("Gus", "Dee", 45), ("Eve", "Finn", 2000), ("Ana", "Ben", 9500),
    ("Ben", "Cruz", 9400), ("Cruz", "Ana", 9300), ("Finn", "Gus", 4950), ("Gus", "Hal", 4900),
    ("Hal", "Finn", 4850),
]

# Each tuple is a payment: who paid, who was paid, and how much (the edge's weight)
payments = ec.Graph.from_edges(edges, directed=True)

payments.plot(label_by="label", seed=38, width=600, height=360)
```
:::

::::: {.ec-queries}

:::: {.ec-step}
[Rings]{.ec-step-name}

Money that goes around a circle of three accounts in large payments, and comes back to where it
started.

```{python}
payments.match("""
    MATCH (a)-[x]->(b)-[y]->(c)-[z]->(a)
    WHERE x.weight >= 1000 AND y.weight >= 1000 AND z.weight >= 1000
      AND a.name < b.name AND a.name < c.name
    RETURN a.name AS a, b.name AS b, c.name AS c
""")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
_hits(
    """MATCH (a)-[x]->(b)-[y]->(c)-[z]->(a)
    WHERE x.weight >= 1000 AND y.weight >= 1000 AND z.weight >= 1000""",
    ["a", "b", "c"],
    ["x", "y", "z"],
)
```
::::

:::: {.ec-step}
[Who pays Eve]{.ec-step-name}

The accounts that pay Eve, and how much, largest first.

```{python}
payments.match("""
    MATCH (a)-[p]->(b {name: "Eve"})
    RETURN a.name AS payer, p.weight AS amount
    ORDER BY amount DESC
""")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
_hits('MATCH (a)-[p]->(b {name: "Eve"})', ["a", "b"], "p")
```
::::

:::: {.ec-step}
[Two hops from Dee]{.ec-step-name}

Everyone Dee's money reaches in one or two payments, with a variable-length pattern.

```{python}
payments.match("""
    MATCH (a {name: "Dee"})-[r*1..2]->(b)
    WHERE b <> a
    RETURN DISTINCT b.name AS reached
""")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
_hits('MATCH (a {name: "Dee"})-[r*1..2]->(b) WHERE b <> a', ["a", "b"], "r")
```
::::

:::: {.ec-step}
[Top senders]{.ec-step-name}

The three accounts that send the most, with aggregation, ordering and a limit.

```{python}
payments.match("""
    MATCH (a)-[p]->()
    RETURN a.name AS account, count(p) AS payments, sum(p.weight) AS total
    ORDER BY total DESC
    LIMIT 3
""")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
_hits(
    """MATCH (a)-[p]->() WITH a, sum(p.weight) AS total ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 3
    MATCH (a)-[q]->()""",
    "a",
    "q",
)
```
::::

:::: {.ec-step}
[Shortest route]{.ec-step-name}

The fewest payments that take money from Ana to Hal, as a path, joined to the node table for the
accounts' names.

```{python}
(
    payments.match("""
        MATCH p = shortestPath((a {name: "Ana"})-[*]->(b {name: "Hal"}))
        RETURN nodes(p) AS id
    """)
    .explode("id")
    .join(payments.get_node_df(), on="id", maintain_order="left")
    .select("id", "label")
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
_hits('MATCH p = shortestPath((a {name: "Ana"})-[r*]->(b {name: "Hal"}))', "p", "r")
```
::::

:::::

::::::

The same patterns drive [selections](user_guide/08-selections.qmd): select what a pattern
matches, or nodes and edges by attribute, degree, centrality or neighborhood, and then set
attributes on them, delete them, [traverse](user_guide/09-traversals.qmd) outward from them, or
take the subgraph they form.

## Every step, recorded {.ec-heading}

A graph keeps a log of the steps taken on it, so an analysis documents itself, and `play()` turns
the log into an animation. This one searches outward from Ana, finds the rings of large payments,
and flags the accounts in them. It plays when it comes into view; pause it, or step through it.

::: {.ec-player}
```{python}
flagged = (
    ec.Graph.from_edges(edges, directed=True)
    .bfs("Ana")
    .select_match("""
        MATCH (a)-[x]->(b)-[y]->(c)-[z]->(a)
        WHERE x.weight >= 1000 AND y.weight >= 1000 AND z.weight >= 1000
    """)
    .set_node_attrs_ws(flag="ring")
    .clear_selection()
)

flagged.play(seed=38)
```
:::

[The step log →](user_guide/26-step-log.qmd){.ec-more}

## Every method, illustrated {.ec-heading}

Nearly every method in the [API reference](reference/index.qmd) opens with a diagram of what it
computes on a small example graph. Here are some of them; pick one to read about it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
_diagrams = [
    "shortest-path", "pagerank", "betweenness-centrality", "cmty-louvain", "k-core",
    "minimum-spanning-tree", "maximum-flow", "greedy-color", "bridges", "articulation-points",
    "count-triangles", "eulerian-circuit", "maximum-weight-matching", "topological-sort",
    "find-cliques", "closeness-centrality", "astar-path", "edge-coloring", "steiner-tree",
    "k-truss", "dominating-set", "traveling-salesman", "minimum-cut", "cmty-leiden",
    "heat-diffusion", "ego-graph", "condensation", "cycle-basis", "bfs-layers",
    "strongly-connected-components", "influence-maximization", "layout-kamada-kawai",
]


def _tile(name):
    method = name.replace("-", "_")
    return (
        f'<a class="ec-tile" href="reference/Graph.{method}.html">'
        f'<img class="ec-only-light" src="assets/graphs/{name}.light.svg" alt="" loading="lazy">'
        f'<img class="ec-only-dark" src="assets/graphs/{name}.dark.svg" alt="" loading="lazy">'
        f'<span class="ec-tile-name">{method}()</span></a>'
    )


_half = (len(_diagrams) + 1) // 2
_rows = [_diagrams[:_half], _diagrams[_half:]]
HTML(
    '<div class="ec-marquee" role="region" aria-label="Diagrams from the API reference">'
    + "".join(
        f'<div class="ec-marquee-row{" ec-reverse" if k else ""}">'
        f'<div class="ec-marquee-track">{"".join(_tile(name) for name in row)}</div></div>'
        for k, row in enumerate(_rows)
    )
    + "</div>"
)
```

## Fast where it counts {.ec-heading}

The core algorithms run in Rust. Here's how long EdgeCase, igraph and NetworkX take for some
common tasks on a co-authorship network of 23,133 scientists (and, for exact betweenness, the
4,941-node US power grid), shown in proportion: watch a race, or pick a task.

```{python}
#| echo: false
_bench = json.loads(Path("assets/readme/benchmarks.json").read_text())


def _time(s):
    return f"{s * 1000:.1f} ms" if s < 1 else f"{s:.2f} s"


_meta = _bench["meta"]
_table = "".join(
    f"<tr><td>{row['task']}</td><td>{_time(row['edgecase'])}</td><td>{_time(row['igraph'])}</td>"
    f"<td>{_time(row['networkx'])}</td></tr>"
    for row in _bench["rows"]
)
HTML(
    f'<div class="ec-race" data-start="Louvain communities" '
    f'data-bench="{html.escape(json.dumps(_bench))}">'
    '<details class="ec-race-table"><summary>All the timings</summary><table>'
    "<thead><tr><th>Task</th><th>EdgeCase</th><th>igraph</th><th>NetworkX</th></tr></thead>"
    f"<tbody>{_table}</tbody></table>"
    f'<p class="ec-race-note">Each time is the best of five runs (three for NetworkX), with the '
    f"results returned to Python, on an {_meta['machine']} with Python {_meta['python']}, "
    f"NetworkX {_meta['networkx']} and igraph {_meta['igraph']}.</p></details></div>"
)
```

Speed doesn't come at the cost of correctness: more than 9,200 tests cover the library, many of
them checking results against NetworkX on the same graphs, and property-based tests generate
random graphs and Cypher queries to check what must always hold.

## Get started {.ec-heading}

Install EdgeCase from PyPI:

```bash
pip install edgecase
```

Then take the [quick start](user_guide/02-quick-start.qmd), a short tour that builds a graph,
analyzes a real social network, draws it, and queries it in only a few lines each, or read the
[User Guide](user_guide/00-get-started.qmd) from the beginning.
:::
